items.excerpt:
The world generated 31.8 trillion kilowatthours (kWh) of electricity in 2025, more than double the 15.1 trillion kWh generated in 2000, according to our recently updated International Energy Statistics data. This growth in global electricity generation is driven by increasing electricity demand from global population and economic growth, and an increase in global median household income.

Coal was the largest global source of electricity generation from 2000 to 2024, increasing 83% from 5.8 trillion kWh to 10.5 trillion kWh. However, the share of the world’s total generation from coal decreased from its peak of 41% in 2007 to 33% in 2025. Generation from renewable energy saw the largest growth between 2000 and 2025, increasing from 2.9 trillion kWh to 10.6 trillion kWh. Renewables made up 19% of the world’s generation mix in 2000 and increased to 34% in 2025, surpassing coal as the largest source of the world’s electricity generation in 2025.

China, the United States, and India have been the three largest electricity generators in the world since 2013. Together these three countries generated 17.3 trillion kWh in 2025, more electricity than the rest of the world combined.

China has a large population and has experienced rapid economic growth since 2000, leading to increasing electricity generation. Fifteen years ago, Google’s story in Colombia began with five people and a clear belief: technology is most meaningful when it serves people’s ideas, projects, and dreams.

Since opening our local office and launching YouTube in Colombia in 2011, we’ve grown together. Over the years, we’ve shared the journey with Colombians from their first search query to their latest prompt. We’ve introduced tools for everyday life and safety — like Android Earthquake Alerts, Google Wallet, Gemini, YouTube Kids and Family Link — and helped showcase local culture through Google Street View imagery across more than 51 cities and landmarks like the Coffee Cultural Landscape.

Today, Colombia’s curiosity and talent continue to inspire us. You can see it in creators like Profe Alex, who started in a classroom in Duitama and now teaches math on YouTube to over 10 million subscribers. You can also see it in young builders like Elvis Better in Soledad and Juan José Tabares in Tuluá — graduates of Impacto Maker, a program supported by Google.org, that trained 75,000 students and teachers in generative AI. items.excerpt:
For emergency physician Dr. José Elías Ortega, 37, his smartwatch was once simply used for counting steps, managing notifications, and keeping time.

But a few years ago, his Galaxy Watch helped him make a critical decision while he was visiting his mother, who lives alone.

One morning after a night shift at the hospital, Dr. José Elías Ortega found his mother on the floor, trying to get up but unable to focus her gaze or respond to him. Drawing on his medical training, he suspected a stroke. Then he thought of his Galaxy Watch and quickly put it on her wrist to check her vital signs.

The watch detected her oxygen saturation was below normal, changing Dr. José Elías Ortega’s initial assessment. He gave her oxygen and took her to the hospital, where the medical team diagnosed her with influenza-related pneumonia. Fortunately, his mother stabilized and was later discharged.

“If I hadn’t had the watch on hand… we wouldn’t have realized her problem was respiratory,” said Dr. José Elías Ortega.

His mother’s rescue was just the beginning of how Galaxy Watch changed his life story. It has also supported Dr. José Elías Ortega through his own journey with thyroid cancer, helping him improve his sleeping and activity habits.

For Dr. José Elías Ortega, both experiences show the value of detecting health signals many can easily miss. Rather than replacing professional medical treatment, such data from wearables informs users of potential health issues so they can seek care sooner.…

items.summary: In 2025, the United States consumed 34 quadrillion British thermal units (quads) of primary energy to deliver 14 quads of electricity sales to end users, with nearly 60% lost. About 95% of the losses came from converting primary energy into electricity, mostly due to lost heat from burning coal and natural gas. The remaining 5% was lost in the course of delivering electricity across grid infrastructure to homes and businesses.
items.excerpt:
To compare production and consumption across different resources, we convert to a common energy metric, British thermal units (Btu), which typically measures the heat content of the fuels such as petroleum, natural gas, and coal that are burned for energy. For energy sources such as hydropower, wind, solar, and geothermal that aren’t combusted to create energy, we apply a constant conversion factor based on the heat content of electricity.

For combustible fuels, EIA uses thermal conversion factors to convert the physical units into heat content values. Because these factors can change based on the specific characteristics of fuels being produced at different points in time, we update our conversion factors each year.

We publish heat content data for more than 30 petroleum products, 4 types of coal, and natural gas. Each fuel has a unique chemistry and heat content, and the heat content can vary based on the different types of fuel in the mix. For example, the heat content of anthracite coal is higher than the heat content of lignite. The aggregate heat content of coal generally varies based on the mix of the different types of coal produced and consumed.

The aggregate heat contents for petroleum consumption and production have declined in recent decades because of decreasing use of residual fuel oil, which has relatively high heat content, and increasing use of fuels with a lower heat content—such as motor gasoline, distillate fuel oil, and hydrocarbon gas liquids.

Today, we’re launching the Humanity’s First Exam (HFE) benchmark on Kaggle to measure how reliably LLMs answer straightforward, everyday questions. Current frontier models excel at complex math, coding, and science, with most benchmarks measuring these domain-specific capability ceilings.

Instead of focusing on whether a model is capable of solving a task once, HFE measures whether models can consistently solve tasks (and slight variations) every single time. The dataset consists of 544 elementary text and image prompts across 20 foundational capabilities. Over the last 6 months, frontier models have made significant progress on HFE.

Explore the live leaderboard, or read our technical report.

To keep the HFE benchmark dataset up to date, we’re inviting the community to help. Join our three-week Kaggle competition through December 15 and submit everyday questions that today’s models still get wrong.

For over 20 years, we have protected 4 billion users and 13 million organizations in Workspace, and critical enterprise and government systems on Google Cloud. From personal and financial records to board materials, regulated workloads, applications, and AI models, those safeguards protect what matters most. Blocking >99.9% of spam, phishing, and malware, alongside encryption and data residency, follows one principle: your data is yours, and you should always know and decide who can access it.

That trust has powered one of the world’s largest developer ecosystems. Workspace APIs now handle more than 2.8 trillion calls a month, and public Google Drive API traffic alone is more than two-and-a-half times the volume of 2022. More than 18 billion reads from Drive each day come from API callers. Traditional REST APIs were built for human-paced apps where a valid OAuth token implied user intent. As AI agents shift from reading information to acting autonomously at machine speed across email, documents, datasets, and cloud infrastructure, a valid token is no longer enough. Policy checks, data boundaries, and human confirmation have to live in the request path.

Today, Workspace MCP servers and the Workspace CLI are generally available alongside Google Cloud Agent Gateway and unified protections across Workspace and Google Cloud. Builders get modern, agent-ready interfaces, and organizations get the visibility and control to adopt AI agents with confidence.

Some limits shape architecture more than any feature does. AWS Lambda launched in 2014 with a 60-second timeout, moved to 5 minutes in 2015 and to 15 minutes in 2018, and then stayed there for eight years. Last week the limit doubled, and in the same week Lambda learned to run on GPUs and gave platform teams their own runtimes. That is a lot of Lambda for one week.

Two other threads ran through the week. A new AWS Local Zone in Bogotá brought AWS infrastructure closer to users in Colombia. And AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS), Amazon Cognito, and Amazon CloudFront each shipped a piece of identity for agents: who an agent is when it shows up at your door, and how little it should be allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

Headlines AWS Local Zone in Bogotá, Colombia – AWS opened a new Local Zone in Bogotá, so you can now run applications that need single-digit millisecond latency closer to users in Colombia. AWS Local Zones place compute, storage, and networking near large metropolitan areas with the same APIs and tools as a Region, for workloads like real-time gaming, live streaming, and financial transactions. The Bogotá Local Zone supports Amazon EC2 C7i, M7i, and R7i instances, Amazon EBS gp3, gp2, and io1 volumes with local snapshots, Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, AWS Direct Connect, and Application Load Balancer. Two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to look for signs of planets in public telescope data. Now they’ve given professional astronomers a few places to look more closely.

Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system⁠ since the first ones were announced in 1992⁠. A worldwide community of amateur astronomers has long been part of that search. Some comb through public telescope data for small, repeated dips in a star’s brightness that could signal an orbiting planet. Others use their own telescopes to watch for the next dip and share what they see with researchers.

Astronomers have used AI in this search for years. In 2017, researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope⁠ that astronomers had already examined. From those examples, the model learned to recognize which patterns in starlight were most likely to come from a planet. When the researchers used it to examine weaker signals, one led them to an eighth planet orbiting a star called Kepler-90⁠.
